final_proof:
Assume first that \(a<b\). Since \(f\) is continuous on the compact interval \([a,b]\), it is Riemann integrable on every subinterval of \([a,b]\), and hence
\[
F(x)=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt
\]
is well-defined for every \(x\in[a,b]\).

Fix \(x\in(a,b)\). Whenever \(h\ne0\) is sufficiently small that \(x+h\in[a,b]\), additivity of the definite integral (using the usual orientation convention if \(h<0\)) gives
\[
\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}{h}=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}f(t)\,dt.
\]
Since
\[
f(x)=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}f(x)\,dt,
\]
it follows that
\[
\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h-f(x)
=\frac1h\int_x^{x+h}\bigl(f(t)-f(x)\bigr)\,dt.
\]
For either sign of \(h\), the standard integral estimate therefore yields
\[
\left|\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h-f(x)\right|
\le \sup_{t\text{ between }x\text{ and }x+h}|f(t)-f(x)|.
\]
Let \(\varepsilon>0\). By continuity of \(f\) at \(x\), there is \(\delta>0\) such that \(|f(t)-f(x)|<\varepsilon\) for every \(t\in[a,b]\) satisfying \(|t-x|<\delta\). If \(0<|h|<\delta\), every \(t\) between \(x\) and \(x+h\) satisfies \(|t-x|<\delta\). The preceding estimate is thus at most \(\varepsilon\). Consequently
\[
F'(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{F(x+h)-F(x)}h=f(x).
\]
As \(x\in(a,b)\) was arbitrary, \(F'=f\) throughout \((a,b)\).

If derivatives on a closed interval are defined to include one-sided endpoint derivatives, the identical argument with \(h>0\) at \(a\) and \(h<0\) at \(b\) gives
\[
F'_+(a)=\lim_{h\downarrow0}\frac1h\int_a^{a+h}f(t)\,dt=f(a)
\]
and
\[
F'_-(b)=\lim_{h\uparrow0}\frac1h\int_b^{b+h}f(t)\,dt=f(b).
\]
Therefore \(F\) is a primitive of \(f\) on \([a,b]\). If the degenerate interval \(a=b\) is allowed, its interior is empty, so the primitive condition is vacuous under the usual definition.
